title: How Kickstarter Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how Kickstarter works: a crowdfunding site launched in 2009 for creative projects, with all-or-nothing funding goals and a 5 percent commission on successful campaigns. They cover its origins (Perry Chen, Yancey Strickler, Charles Adler), the rules for creative projects and rewards, notable successes and controversies (Veronica Mars movie, Zach Braff film, Coolest Cooler, Zach Danger Brown's potato salad, Chipotle burrito graph), reward-level math, tips for successful campaigns, and a Cambridge study on backer behavior. The episode closes with a listener mail about the phrase "won't play in Peoria."

segments.title: Opening banter and Kickstarter introduction
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about independent creators, DIY equipment, and funding needs, then introduce Kickstarter as a crowdfunding site launched in 2009 to help artists without corporate backing.

segments.title: Crowdsourcing, crowdfunding and early precursors
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh define crowdsourcing and crowdfunding, mention micro patronage and Kiva, and note DonorsChoose and early sites like Indiegogo.

segments.title: Kickstarter origins and rules
segments.summary: Perry Chen, with Yancey Strickler and Charles Adler, founded Kickstarter in 2009 after the idea arose around funding a New Orleans concert. The site allows only creative projects, not paying bills, and requires specific project plans.

segments.title: All-or-nothing funding and the 5 percent commission
segments.summary: Kickstarter uses an all-or-nothing model where creators collect pledges only if they meet the goal, and Kickstarter takes a five percent commission on successful projects. The hosts explain why this protects both creators and backers.

segments.title: Rewards, pledge rules, and creative project definitions
segments.summary: Backers receive rewards, but projects cannot offer equity or financial returns. Creators must complete projects and fulfill rewards. Kickstarter defines creative categories and staff review proposals, which they describe as an evolving standard.

segments.title: Notable successes: Coolest Cooler, watch band, and category stats
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the iPod nano watch band that raised far beyond its goal, the Coolest Cooler's huge success, and statistics on funded project categories and total pledges.

segments.title: Quirky projects: potato salad, Chipotle graph, meat soap
segments.summary: Examples of unusual Kickstarter projects include Zach Danger Brown's potato salad, a Chipotle chicken burrito deliciousness graph, meat soap, and a grizzly bear coat.

segments.title: Tips for successful campaigns and reward-level math
segments.summary: Advice covers strong pitch videos, an anchor audience of friends and social media, reward tier math (the $25 level is most popular, $100 pledges have the biggest dollar impact), and calculating a goal that includes the 5 percent commission.

segments.title: Veronica Mars and Zach Braff controversies
segments.summary: The Veronica Mars movie raised about five million dollars but faced complaints about download delivery through Flixster, which Warner Brothers helped address. Zach Braff's film drew criticism for raising money on Kickstarter despite having other financing, and he said he kept final cut.

segments.title: Cambridge study on Kickstarter backers
segments.summary: Cambridge University computer scientists analyzed three months of Kickstarter data and found frequent and occasional funders respond to different project traits, with quality remaining the key factor.

segments.title: Listener mail: won't play in Peoria
segments.summary: A listener explains the origin of the phrase 'won't play in Peoria' as tied to Peoria, Illinois, a city used as a tryout market for shows before Chicago.
